title: One-dimensional wave equation
lead: A guitar string fixed at both ends moves by the wave equation, which needs the string’s initial shape and its initial velocity. Splitting the problem in two and separating variables gives each half a series of building blocks, a plucked string shows what the series does in time, and its frequencies explain the timbre of the note.

derivations.source: Notes on Diffy Qs, 4.7 One-dimensional wave equation: the problem (4.11) solved by separation of variables

then.why: The wave equation that $w$ solves in (4.11).

steps.cap: Again, the left-hand side depends only on $t$ and the right-hand side depends only on $x$. So both sides equal a constant, which we denote by $-\lambda$.

assumes.text: The problem $X'' + \lambda X = 0$, $X(0) = 0$, $X(L) = 0$ has nontrivial solutions only for $\lambda = \lambda_n = \frac{n^2\pi^2}{L^2}$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, and they are multiples of $\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)$.

steps.cap: The condition $0 = w(0,t) = X(0) T(t)$ implies $X(0) = 0$ and $w(L,t) = 0$ implies that $X(L) = 0$.

assumes.text: The general solution of $T'' + \omega^2 T = 0$ is $T = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t)$.
It is convenient to pick $B = \frac{L}{n \pi a}$ (you will see why in a moment).

steps.cap: With $\omega = \frac{n\pi a}{L}$ this is the general solution for $T$ for this particular $\lambda_n$.
The condition $w(x,0) = 0$, or $X(x)T(0) = 0$, implies that $T(0) = 0$, which in turn forces $A = 0$.

then.why: Our building-block solutions are the products $X_n(x)T_n(t)$.

assumes.text: Superposition: a sum of solutions of the wave equation and of the homogeneous side conditions is again a solution.

then.why: We expand $g(x)$ in terms of the sines $\frac{\partial w_n}{\partial t}(x,0)$, and using superposition we write the solution as a series with the same coefficients.

derivations.source: Notes on Diffy Qs, 4.7 One-dimensional wave equation: the problem (4.12) solved by separation of variables

assumes.text: The general solution of $T'' + \omega^2 T = 0$ is $T = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t)$.

then.why: We obtain the same two equations as for (4.11), and the conditions $X(0) = 0$, $X(L) = 0$; again $\lambda = \lambda_n$.

steps.cap: This time, the condition on $T$ is $T'(0) = 0$, since $z_t(x,0) = X(x)T'(0) = 0$. As $T_n'(0) = \frac{n\pi a}{L}B$, we get that $B = 0$, and we take $A = 1$.

then.why: Our building-block solution is the product $X_n(x)T_n(t)$.

assumes.text: Superposition: a sum of solutions of the wave equation and of the homogeneous side conditions is again a solution.

then.why: As $z_n(x,0) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)$, we expand $f(x)$ in terms of these sines, and superposition writes the solution as a series with the same coefficients.

answer.solution: Every term of $\kw(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \kbn \frac{L}{n \pi a} \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right) \sin\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right)$ has the factor $\sin\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right)$, which is $\sin 0 = 0$ at $t = 0$, so $\kw(x,0) = 0$. Differentiating term by term in $t$, the chain rule brings out $\frac{n\pi a}{L}$, which cancels the $\frac{L}{n\pi a}$: $w_t(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \kbn \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right) \cos\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right)$. At $t = 0$, $\cos 0 = 1$, so $w_t(x,0) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \kbn \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right) = \kg(x)$, the sine series of $\kg$. This is why $B = \frac{L}{n\pi a}$ was the convenient choice.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the details in the derivation of the solution of (4.12). Check that the solution satisfies all the side conditions.

answer.solution: Putting $\kz = \kX(x)\kT(t)$ into $z_{tt} = a^2 z_{xx}$ gives $\kX\kTdprime = a^2\kXdprime\kT$, so $\frac{\kTdprime}{a^2\kT} = -\klambda = \frac{\kXdprime}{\kX}$, that is $\kXdprime + \klambda\kX = 0$ and $\kTdprime + \klambda a^2\kT = 0$. The ends give $0 = \kz(0,t) = \kX(0)\kT(t)$ and likewise at $L$, so $\kX(0) = \kX(L) = 0$, hence $\klambdan = \frac{n^2\pi^2}{L^2}$ and $\kXn = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)$, and $\kTn = A\cos\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right) + B\sin\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right)$. The condition $z_t(x,0) = \kX(x)\kTprime(0) = 0$ needs $\kTprime(0) = \frac{n\pi a}{L}B = 0$, so $B = 0$; taking $A = 1$, $\kzn = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\cos\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right)$. Now check $\kz = \sum \kcn \kzn$: each $\kzn$ has $(\kzn)_{tt} = -\frac{n^2\pi^2a^2}{L^2}\kzn = a^2(\kzn)_{xx}$, so $\kz$ solves the equation by superposition; $\kz(0,t) = \kz(L,t) = 0$ because $\sin 0 = \sin(n\pi) = 0$; $\kz(x,0) = \sum \kcn \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right) = \kf(x)$ because $\cos 0 = 1$; and $z_t(x,0) = -\sum \kcn \frac{n\pi a}{L} \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right) \sin 0 = 0$.

exercises.prompt:
Solve

$$ \begin{array}{ll} \kytt = 9 \kyxx & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ \ky(0,t) = \ky(1,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ \ky(x,0) = \sin (3\pi x) + \frac{1}{4} \sin (6 \pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 , \\ \kyt(x,0) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 . \end{array} $$

answer.solution: $\ky(x,t) = \sin(3\pi x)\cos(9\pi t) + \frac{1}{4}\sin(6\pi x)\cos(18\pi t)$. Here $L = 1$, $a = 3$ and $\kg = 0$, so every $\kbn = 0$. The initial shape is already a sine series, with $c_3 = 1$, $c_6 = \frac{1}{4}$ and every other $\kcn = 0$. By Theorem 4.7.1 each term $\kcn\sin(n\pi x)$ moves as $\kcn\sin(n\pi x)\cos(n\pi a t) = \kcn\sin(n\pi x)\cos(3n\pi t)$, which gives the answer. Check: both terms satisfy $\kytt = 9\kyxx$ and vanish at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, and at $t = 0$ the sum is the initial shape with $\kyt(x,0) = 0$.

exercises.prompt:
Solve

$$ \begin{array}{ll} \kytt = 4 \kyxx & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ \ky(0,t) = \ky(1,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ \ky(x,0) = \sin (3\pi x) + \frac{1}{4} \sin (6 \pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 , \\ \kyt(x,0) = \sin (9 \pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 . \end{array} $$

answer.solution: $\ky(x,t) = \sin(3\pi x)\cos(6\pi t) + \frac{1}{4}\sin(6\pi x)\cos(12\pi t) + \frac{1}{18\pi}\sin(9\pi x)\sin(18\pi t)$. Here $L = 1$ and $a = 2$. The shape gives $c_3 = 1$, $c_6 = \frac{1}{4}$, the velocity gives $b_9 = 1$, and every other coefficient is zero. By Theorem 4.7.1 the $\kcn$ terms carry $\cos(n\pi a t) = \cos(2n\pi t)$, and the $b_9$ term is $b_9\frac{L}{9\pi a}\sin(9\pi x)\sin(9\pi a t) = \frac{1}{18\pi}\sin(9\pi x)\sin(18\pi t)$. Check: each term satisfies $\kytt = 4\kyxx$ and vanishes at both ends; at $t = 0$ the sum is the initial shape, and its $t$-derivative there is $\sin(9\pi x)$.

exercises.prompt: Derive the solution for a general plucked string of length $L$ and any constant $a$ (in the equation $\kytt = a^2 \kyxx$), where we raise the string some distance $b$ at the midpoint and let go.

answer.solution: $\ky(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{8b}{n^2\pi^2}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\cos\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right) = \sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{8b{(-1)}^{m+1}}{{(2m-1)}^2\pi^2}\sin\left(\frac{(2m-1)\pi}{L}x\right)\cos\left(\frac{(2m-1)\pi a}{L}t\right)$. The initial shape is the triangle $\kf(x) = \frac{2b}{L}x$ for $0 \leq x \leq \frac{L}{2}$ and $\kf(x) = \frac{2b}{L}(L - x)$ for $\frac{L}{2} < x \leq L$, and the string is let go at rest, so $\kg = 0$ and every $\kbn = 0$. The sine coefficients are $\kcn = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L \kf(x)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)dx = \frac{8b}{n^2\pi^2}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)$, integrating by parts on each half (the boundary terms cancel at $\frac{L}{2}$, and each half contributes $\frac{4b}{n^2\pi^2}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)$). Theorem 4.7.1 then gives the series; only odd $n$ appear, with alternating signs. With $L = 2$, $b = 0.1$ and $a = 1$ it is Example 4.7.1.

exercises.prompt: Imagine that a stringed musical instrument fell on the floor. Suppose that the length of the string is 1 and $a=1$. When the musical instrument hit the ground, the string was in rest position and hence $\ky(x,0) = 0$. However, the string was moving at some velocity at impact ($t=0$), say $\kyt(x,0) = -1$. Find the solution $\ky(x,t)$ for the shape of the string at time $t$.

answer.solution: $\ky(x,t) = \sum_{n \text{ odd}} \frac{-4}{n^2\pi^2}\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi t) = -\frac{4}{\pi^2}\left(\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi t) + \frac{1}{9}\sin(3\pi x)\sin(3\pi t) + \frac{1}{25}\sin(5\pi x)\sin(5\pi t) + \cdots\right)$. Here $L = 1$, $a = 1$, $\kf = 0$, so every $\kcn = 0$, and $\kg = -1$. The sine series of $-1$ on $0 < x < 1$ has $\kbn = 2\int_0^1 (-1)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx = \frac{2\bigl((-1)^n - 1\bigr)}{n\pi}$, which is $-\frac{4}{n\pi}$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$. By Theorem 4.7.1, $\ky = \sum \kbn\frac{L}{n\pi a}\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi t) = \sum \kbn\frac{1}{n\pi}\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi t)$, which gives the answer. The string sags and comes back: at $t = \frac{1}{2}$ its middle is at $-\frac{1}{2}$, and at $t = 1$ it is flat again, moving up.

exercises.prompt:
challenging Suppose that you have a vibrating string and that there is air resistance proportional to the velocity. That is, you have

$$ \begin{array}{ll} \kytt = a^2 \kyxx - k \kyt & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ \ky(0,t) = \ky(1,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ \ky(x,0) = \kf(x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 , \\ \kyt(x,0) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 . \end{array} $$

Suppose that $0 < k < 2 \pi a$. Derive a series solution to the problem. Any coefficients in the series should be expressed as integrals of $\kf(x)$.

answer.solution: $\ky(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \kcn\, e^{-kt/2}\left(\cos(\omega_n t) + \frac{k}{2\omega_n}\sin(\omega_n t)\right)\sin(n\pi x)$, with $\omega_n = \sqrt{n^2\pi^2a^2 - \frac{k^2}{4}}$ and $\kcn = 2\int_0^1 \kf(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx$. With $\ky = \kX(x)\kT(t)$ the equation $\kX\kTdprime = a^2\kXdprime\kT - k\kX\kTprime$ separates as $\frac{\kTdprime + k\kTprime}{a^2\kT} = \frac{\kXdprime}{\kX} = -\klambda$. The ends give $\kX(0) = \kX(1) = 0$, so $\klambdan = n^2\pi^2$ and $\kXn = \sin(n\pi x)$, and then $\kTdprime + k\kTprime + n^2\pi^2a^2\kT = 0$. Its characteristic roots are $-\frac{k}{2} \pm i\omega_n$, and $\omega_n$ is real for every $n \geq 1$ because $k < 2\pi a \leq 2n\pi a$, so every mode is underdamped. The condition $\kyt(x,0) = 0$ needs $\kTprime(0) = 0$; with $\kT(0) = 1$ this picks $\kTn(t) = e^{-kt/2}\left(\cos(\omega_n t) + \frac{k}{2\omega_n}\sin(\omega_n t)\right)$, since its derivative at $0$ is $-\frac{k}{2} + \frac{k}{2\omega_n}\omega_n = 0$. By superposition $\ky = \sum \kcn \kXn \kTn$, and $\ky(x,0) = \sum \kcn\sin(n\pi x) = \kf(x)$ when the $\kcn$ are the sine coefficients of $\kf$ above.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you touch the guitar string exactly in the middle to ensure another condition $\ky({L}/{2},t) = 0$ for all time. Which multiples of the fundamental frequency $\frac{\pi a}{L}$ show up in the solution?

answer.solution: Only the even multiples, $\frac{2\pi a}{L}, \frac{4\pi a}{L}, \frac{6\pi a}{L}, \ldots$ At $x = \frac{L}{2}$ the solution of Theorem 4.7.1 is $\ky\left(\frac{L}{2},t\right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)\left[\kbn\frac{L}{n\pi a}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right) + \kcn\cos\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}t\right)\right]$. For even $n$, $\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right) = 0$; for odd $n$ it is $\pm 1$. This is a Fourier series in $t$, and it is zero for all time only if every coefficient is zero, so $\kbn = \kcn = 0$ for every odd $n$. What is left are the even $n$, the frequencies $n\frac{\pi a}{L}$ for $n = 2, 4, 6, \ldots$: each half of the string vibrates as a string of length $\frac{L}{2}$, whose fundamental frequency is $\frac{2\pi a}{L}$.
